text:
Developments within the city limits during the 1850's included hotels, grocery stores, a photograph gallery, a book shop, a drug store, a jewelry store, a candy factory, a brewery, a bakery, a flour mill, a clothing store, a harness shop, a distillery, and the valley's first newspaper. Two private schools, the first public school and San Jose State College were also founded during this decade (Arbuckle 1948; Winther 1935).
On January 18, 1864 the first train service between San Francisco and San Jose began. The resulting boom to the city was almost equal to that associated with the gold rush. Real estate immediately increased in value and the construction of new establishments began anew. More hotels, restaurants, bowling alleys, livery stables, saloons, and merchandising stores were completed. Soon to follow were banks, a silk factory, flour, lumber, and woolen mills, breweries, and dry goods stores. During the late sixties the City completed a $200,000.00 court house, new schools, a new water and sewage system, a city park, and the laying out of East San Jose under a homestead act. By 1860 the population of San Jose had surpassed the 12,000 mark (Hall 1871; Winther 1935).
Once established, the City of San Jose soon became the center for agricultural activities in the Santa Clara Valley. During the 1850's and 1860's the Valley had shifted its emphasis from cattle raising to wheat production. Wheat would remain as the dominant industry of the Santa Clara Valley until the 1870's when continuous monocropping of soils would cause wheat production to peak and decline. A shift to horticulture occurred during the 1870's and 1880's. Orchard and row crops soon dominated the Valley and continued to do so until the present period of urban expansion (Hickman, 1974).
Alviso
The beginnings of Alviso can be traced to the year 1849 when a French immigrant named Haro pitched a tent on what was to become the center of the town (Munro-Fraser 1881). Prior to this date the Alviso town site was encompassed by the Rancho Rincon de los Esteros of Ygnacio Alviso who had received a land grant of 6,362 acres in 1838. The Alviso adobe was constructed approximately one mile southeast of the town site on the east bank of the Guadalupe River. From 1835 to 1849 the southern tip of the San Francisco Bay was known as the Embarcadero de Santa Clara. At a point on the Guadalupe River one-half mile above Alviso was a landing where tons of Santa Clara Valley cow hides, tallow, and quicksilver from the Almaden mines were shipped to San Francisco (Arbuckle 1948, 1968).
